clue.text: No credit goes to this author-he got wrist trouble, right?

definitions.text: No credit goes to this author

indicators.note: trouble suggests the letters of these words are disturbed and thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: An injured writer complains of a sore wrist and asks whether that is fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges HEGOTWRIST into GHOSTWRITE, and R for 'right' is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired writer produces books published under someone else's name, receiving no byline or credit.
Regular means usual or widespread, as in the overall picture; an army officer of high rank holds this title.

parts.note: styles that are no longer current are said to be out
a do is an informal word for a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A team beats its rivals at an outdated sort of party.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat or surpass someone is to triumph over them.

parts.note: a top is a toy that spins on its point
a hole is a gap or opening

explanation.surface: An exclamation praising a bowler who starts the innings with spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spinner' suggests cricket spin bowling, but here it is the toy. TOPHOLE is old British slang for first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated British slang for excellent or first-rate.
Rocket is a salad herb, also a firework that shoots skyward, and to get a rocket is British slang for being told off.

clue.text: Where to see beginning and end of the rainbow?

definitions.text: Where to see beginning and end of the rainbow?

parts.words: Where to see beginning and end of the rainbow?
parts.note: the rainbow is a kind of fish, reared from birth until it is harvested at one establishment

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about where a rainbow in the sky starts and stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish farm raises rainbow trout from hatchery to slaughter, so their whole lives are spent there.

clue.text: Given ground, put out to grass

explanation.definitionFit: An army that gave ground has withdrawn; someone put out to grass has stopped working, like an old horse sent to pasture.
Unbroken means continuous; carrying on without a pause is the opposite of taking a break.

parts.note: night is the dark part of the day
porter is a dark beer, a kind of ale

explanation.surface: Someone bringing round a dark beer, perhaps after the pub has closed.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel employee who works through the small hours, carrying luggage and serving guests late on.

indicators.note: a firm going bust collapses, so these letters break up and reassemble

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A watch company is collapsing financially.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' looks like an adjective but is a noun: a Native American warrior. The anagram of WATCHCO gives CHOCTAW, a Native American people.
explanation.definitionFit: A brave is a Native American warrior, and the Choctaw are a Native American nation.

indicators.note: settled suggests these words are arranged anew, as a dispute is sorted out

explanation.surface: Liberal-minded politicians have agreed the conditions in the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wets' is British slang for weak or moderate politicians, helping the surface. 'Settled' rearranges WETSTERMSIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The British legislature sits in the Palace of this London district, so its name stands for Parliament itself.

clue.text: Former film-star who sought isolation in dress-circle

parts.note: garb is clothing or dress
the letter O is shaped like a circle

explanation.surface: A retired actress wanted solitude in the theatre's upper seating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dress-circle' looks like one theatre term but splits into two pieces. Greta Garbo famously said she wanted to be alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Greta Garbo, the Swedish screen star, retired early and was famous for shunning publicity.

clue.text: Openings of Hamlet and Coriolanus, for example?

definitions.text: Openings of Hamlet and Coriolanus, for example?

parts.words: Openings of Hamlet and Coriolanus, for example?
parts.note: not the first scenes of the plays but orchestral works named after them, by Tchaikovsky and Beethoven

explanation.surface: The first lines of two Shakespeare tragedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky's Hamlet and Beethoven's Coriolan are concert pieces of the kind that open an opera.

parts.note: till means until or up to
eighteen is the age of majority, when one comes of age

explanation.surface: A farm labourer works until he turns eighteen.
explanation.walkthrough: '18' looks like a cross-reference to another entry, but it stands for coming of age.
explanation.definitionFit: Cultivating land by ploughing and harrowing is what a farmhand does.

clue.text: Divorced fellows with time in flat, perhaps

parts.note: separated, living apart
men are fellows or chaps

explanation.surface: Separated men spend time living in a small flat.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat is one example of a set of rooms forming a home, the American term.

clue.text: Fame of retired moderates with no signs of energy

indicators.note: E is the physics symbol for energy, and every one of them is removed from the reversed word
retired means withdrawn or gone back, so the word moderates is written backwards

explanation.surface: Moderate politicians who have retired lose fame and have no energy left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns MODERATES into SETAREDOM; 'with no signs of energy' takes out both Es.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity status is the condition of being renowned.

indicators.note: following means the worker comes after the cricket side

parts.note: the off side is one half of a cricket field
a hand is a manual worker

explanation.surface: A labourer casually follows a cricket team.
explanation.walkthrough: The off side in cricket is the half of the field on the batter's bat side.
explanation.definitionFit: An offhand remark is casual, made without thought or care.

clue.text: Weakness of female, not feeling well

parts.note: ailing means sick or unwell

explanation.surface: A woman who feels poorly shows a frailty.
explanation.definitionFit: A failing is a fault or shortcoming in character.

clue.text: US conscript exposed to air-currents, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word for breezy is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a draughty room lets in cold currents of air

explanation.surface: An American recruit standing in a chilly breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: DRAUGHTY is the British spelling; said aloud it matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone drafted is called up for military service in America.

parts.note: to bump is to knock or hit
kin means relatives or family

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone struck a relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumpkin is an unsophisticated country person, a yokel.
A billet is a ticket or note (French billet) and also lodgings assigned to soldiers.

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of the two names are put out of order

explanation.surface: Telling Tony to stretch the supply of tonic water further.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tonic' suggests a drink, but in music it is the first note of a scale; 'out' rearranges TONYEKE.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the key note is the first degree of the scale, also called the tonic.

clue.text: Perhaps at thrilly stage in final set?

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters may be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A tense moment in the deciding set of a tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges ATTHRILLY. In tennis, thirty-all is the score when both players have two points.
explanation.definitionFit: A level score in a tennis game, two points each, at a gripping moment of the deciding set.

parts.note: to cry is to call out or announce

explanation.surface: A gym instructor announces a session on the vaulting horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vault' suggests the gymnastics jump; here it is an underground chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: An underground chamber beneath a church, often used for burials.

indicators.note: put on means the one is added after the fur

parts.note: a fur is a coat
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone putting on a fur coat.
explanation.definitionFit: A coati is a raccoon-like mammal of the Americas.

indicators.note: in places the design inside the word for torn

parts.note: rent means torn or ripped
an aim is a purpose or design

explanation.surface: A pattern on ripped clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiment is an old, literary word for garments.

indicators.note: all round suggests the letters are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Our name is displayed all around the doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' reads as a doorway but is the verb, stress on the second syllable: to enchant.
explanation.definitionFit: To charm or captivate someone is to fill them with love.

parts.note: a gutter is a channel for water
a snipe is a wading bird of marshes

explanation.surface: A drain and a wading bird, both found in muddy places.
explanation.definitionFit: A mudlark is a street urchin who scavenges, a ragged child of the slums.
